units: a hard surface sends a short jolt back into the foot as it lands
that jolt travels up through the ankle joint and then the joints of the leg
the muscles soak up part of the impact, which brings on exhaustion sooner
stride length shortens on its own over that kind of surface
the foot then lands closer to the hips
a shorter stride covers less ground and brings the pace down
the body speeds up its step rate to make up for it, at the cost of heavier breathing
coaches advise rotating training surfaces
repeating one identical movement on one identical surface injures more than the distance covered
text: Land on a hard surface and the foot takes back a short, sharp jolt. It climbs from the sole up into the ankle, and from there on into the knee and the hip. Because the muscle soaks up part of that energy, tiredness shows up a good deal sooner than it would on soft ground. The stride then shortens all by itself. The foot comes down closer to the hips, and the joint takes less strain for it. Shorter steps mean less ground covered per stride, so the pace falls off. To make that up, the body turns the legs over faster, and the extra turnover costs more breath. Coaches therefore tell their runners to rotate surfaces from one session to the next. Soft footing gives a tendon room to recover, while firm footing builds up bone. What injures a runner is not the distance covered. It is doing the same movement over and over on the same surface.

units: the club coach kept warning that ankles would give out before lungs
ground hardened by the cold kept the shoes from gripping
half the squad limped when the season started up again
the players blamed their gear, then the man who ran the gym, then bad luck
one player who works as a physical therapist suggested a balance drill on one foot
the drill is done on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall, before every session
the players thought the drill was ridiculous at first
sprains grew rarer once the habit took hold
the routine now opens every session, whatever shape the ground is in
text: Our coach kept telling us our ankles would quit before our lungs did, and he was right. As soon as the cold hardened the ground, the shoes stopped biting, and half the squad limped through the first weeks back. We blamed the shoes. Then we blamed the man who ran the gym. Then we blamed plain bad luck. One of us, a physical therapist by trade, offered a deal: a quarter of an hour balancing on one foot before every session, on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall. Nobody bought it. At first we laughed at each other wobbling like badly planted fence posts. Then the sprains thinned out, and coming back after the break stopped feeling like a sick ward. The drill has opened every session since, frozen ground, soaked ground or dry. Our coach never once admitted he had not thought of it himself.

units: three kinds of sole stand apart when you shop
the thick, soft sole cushions the impact and suits long outings on the road
the thick sole wears out fast and leaves the foot unsteady going downhill
the thin sole brings the foot closer to the ground and passes the push through better
the thin sole leaves the tendon open to repeated jolts
the studded sole is meant for soft ground and turns uncomfortable on a hard track
trying models on is advised once the foot has already swollen
you should jog on a firm surface before closing the sale
ankle support is tested by pivoting in place
text: Buying an athletic shoe comes down to weighing three kinds of sole, say the salespeople trained for the job. The first runs thick and soft. It cushions the impact and suits long outings on pavement, though it wears out fast and leaves the foot unsteady on a downhill. The second one is thinner. It brings the foot nearer the ground and passes the push through better, but it leaves the tendon open to jolt after jolt. The third carries studs and belongs on soft ground. On a hard track it turns loud and awkward underfoot. The method the sellers advise takes three moves. Try the models on once the foot has swollen from a long walk. Jog on a firm surface before you reach for your card. Then pivot in place and compare how each one holds the ankle. A shoe that fits draws far less notice than one that pinches.

units: the gym reopens after its equipment was overhauled
the tumbling floor has been rebuilt from scratch
a springboard stands in front of the vaulting table
the bars carry the chalk left on them by the athletes
the hanging rings serve mainly for upper-body strength work
a pit filled with foam blocks catches the falls of those still learning
beginners show up late in the evening
attendance has risen since the reopening
the people who run the place credit the renewed equipment
text: A smell of varnish still hangs over the mats in the entrance of the overhauled gym. The tumbling floor, rebuilt from scratch, gives back a flat sound under a visitor's shoe. Then comes the springboard, a curved plank the vaulters test with a heel before they trust it. Farther along, the bars carry the white streaks of chalk that every athlete leaves behind in passing. The rings hang from the ceiling on long cables and serve mostly for upper-body strength work. At the far end, a pit of foam blocks takes the falls of anyone still learning, and the dull thud it gives off marks out the hours of the evening. Beginners turn up late, when the room still belongs to quiet. Attendance has climbed steadily since the doors opened again, and the people who run the place credit the renewed equipment.

units: the run-up sets the speed of arrival on the board
the jumper builds speed gradually while keeping the chest upright
the second-to-last step serves to lower the center of gravity
the last contact with the ground lasts less time than the ones before
that last contact turns forward speed into an upward push
the board bends under the load and then gives back the energy it stored
the arms rise at the moment the board returns the jumper
the rotation starts during the rise and not after the high point
a landing that is too stiff passes the shock into the ankle joint
text: Everything starts with the run-up, whose length sets the speed of arrival on the board. The jumper builds pace gradually, chest upright, stride even. On the second-to-last step, the supporting leg bends further and the center of gravity drops. The final contact with the ground lasts less time than the ones before it. That is the contact that turns forward speed into an upward push. The board bends under the load, then hands back the energy it stored. The arms come up at that exact moment, or the drive leaks away. Rotation begins during the rise, never after the high point of the flight. The landing takes both feet, knees bent, chest tipped slightly forward. A landing too stiff passes the shock straight into the ankle and the tendon, which accounts for most of the injuries seen at this stage.

units: nothing requires a child to settle on one discipline before adolescence
early specialization piles the same movements onto the same joints
that concentration brings on tendon overload before growth is finished
a narrow movement repertoire makes adapting hard when the ground changes
boredom is put forward as the leading cause of dropping out
clubs push specialization because early results attract funding
the writer proposes delaying selection in the youth categories
he recommends requiring a second activity of every competitor
text: Nothing requires a child to settle on a single discipline before adolescence, yet clubs press for it anyway, and the effects can be measured. Early specialization piles the same movements onto the same joints, so tendon overload appears well before growth has finished. It also narrows the movement repertoire. A teenager who has known one apparatus, or one kind of footing, adapts poorly the moment the ground changes. Then comes boredom, the leading cause of dropping out between late childhood and adulthood. Clubs persist because results that arrive early attract funding. We would gain by pushing selection later in the youth categories and by asking every competitor to take up a second activity. An athletic career rests on the variety of the supports it is built from, not on their repetition.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the strength coach was a competitive swimmer when she was young
a torn tendon cut her athletic career short
she went back to school after that injury
she noticed that injuries mostly happened on the return after a break
she set up a build-up spread over three weeks
that build-up begins with light loads and slowed-down movements
heavy loads come in only at the end of that period
the number of injuries fell at her club
neighboring clubs have taken up her method
text: They call her the club's strength coach, and her whole office fits inside a single gym bag set down at the edge of the pool. She swam in competition as a young woman, until the evening a tendon tore and her career ended on the spot. She went back to school after that injury, then came back to the water with a question in her head. Watching her athletes closely, she noticed that injuries rarely struck in the middle of the season. They struck on the return, after a break. So she imposed a build-up spread over three weeks, made of light loads and movements deliberately slowed down. Heavy weights enter only at the end of that stretch, once the ankle and the shoulder have their full range back. The injury count at her club fell away, and the clubs nearby now copy what she does.

units: the writer went to two gyms over the same season
the first gym is fitted with guided machines and with screens
the guided machines force the movement along a fixed path
the second gym sits in a poorly heated shed
the second gym offers mostly bars, free weights and apparatus
the coach at the second gym fixes your position without being asked
the writer made more progress in the less comfortable gym
he still recommends the plush gym to anyone the iron intimidates
text: I went to two gyms this season, and they have almost nothing in common. The first one gleams: guided machines, screens everywhere, soft music, carpet that swallows the sound of the weights. It feels good in there, except the machine picks the path for you, and the shoulder never learns to hold itself. The second one sits in a badly heated shed, with bars, free weights and a couple of squeaking apparatus. The floor rings, people talk loudly, and the coach walks straight over to fix your position without waiting to be asked. Guess where I got stronger. In the shed, obviously, because a whole movement beats one that is steered along rails. I would still send anyone the iron intimidates to the plush place. A reassuring machine beats giving the whole thing up after a single week.

units: the writer reports to her reader on the club she joined
the adult section's sessions last an hour and a half
the warm-up takes the first third of the session
the equipment includes thick mats, a springboard and two sets of weights
the membership fee covers the loan of studded shoes
the staff is made up of two volunteers and one paid employee
the paid employee follows up on the athletes who get hurt
newcomers sit in on two sessions before paying
the writer invites her reader to come one weekday evening
text: Dear neighbor, you asked me for a proper report on the club I joined, so here it is. Sessions in the adult section run an hour and a half, and a full third of that goes to the warm-up, which surprised me at first and won me over later on. The equipment holds up well: thick mats, a springboard in good shape, and two sets of weights, from the lightest to the heaviest. The fee covers the loan of studded shoes, which matters a lot if you would rather buy nothing until you are sure. Staffing rests on two volunteers and one paid employee, and she is the one who follows the athletes who get hurt, a twisted ankle, an angry tendon. Newcomers sit in on two sessions before they pay a thing. Tuesday evenings are quiet, so come along to one and I will introduce you to the whole group.

units: the first question is about what happens as the wall comes up
the swimmer judges the distance left without lifting his head
he adjusts the reach of his arm strokes to arrive at the right spacing
the flip starts with the chest tipping toward the bottom
the feet land on the wall, set hip width apart
the push off the wall produces a speed higher than swimming does
the tucked position underwater holds that speed
the stroke has to start again before the speed falls away
a badly placed foot costs more than a badly swum length
text: What happens to a swimmer in the second just before the wall? He measures, without ever lifting his head, the distance he has left, and he stretches or shortens his arm strokes so as to arrive neither too close nor too far out from it. And after that? The chest tips over toward the bottom, the flip goes round, and the feet land flat on the wall, set about hip width apart. Does the turn really matter as much as people claim? It does, because the push off the wall throws him forward faster than he will ever swim under his own power. The tucked position underwater holds on to that speed, provided that nothing sticks out. And when should the stroke start again? Just before the speed begins to fall away. A foot set wrong on the wall costs him more than an entire length swum badly.
